(d) the bank-wise NPAs in the country?  
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRI PAWAN 
KUMAR BANSAL ) (a) and (d) As on 31 st March, 2007, the Gross Non-Performing Assets 
(NPAs) of Scheduled Commercial Banks (SCBs) stood a t Rs. 50,552 crore. A statement 
indicating bank-wise details of Gross NPAs of SCBs is given in the Statement. (See below)  
The factors responsible for NPAs, inter-alia, include diversion of funds by the borrower and 
wilful default in repayment, deficiency in credit a ppraisal and supervision, inefficient 
management of the unit financed, poor follow up and monitoring, unviability or sickness of 
the unit due to change in technology demand pattern and other policy etc., non-completion 
of project due to cost, time, overrurns and other f actors, such as non-availability of raw 
materials etc., labour problems,natural calamities, delay in disposal by courts of suits filed by 
banks, etc. However, the banks monitor their loan a ccounts at various levels and take 
appropriate corrective action, on an ongoing basis, to arrest slippages to NPA category. 
Reserve Bank of India (RBI) and the Government of I ndia have taken various steps to 
improve assets quality of the banks which, inter-alia, include prescribing prudential 
norms for provisioning and classification of non-pe rforming assets, guidelines for 
prevention of slippages, introduction of Corporate Debt Restructuring mechanism. One 
Time Settlement schemes, enactment of (i) The Secur itisation and Reconstruction of 
Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Intere st (SARFAESI) Act, 2002, (ii) the 
Credit Information Companies (Regulation) Act, 2005, and (iii) the Recovery of Debts due 
to Banks and Financial Institutions (DRT) Act, 1993, etc. Due to concerted efforts, the net 
NPAs of the SCBs have declined from 4.4% of Net Adv ances as on 31st March, 2003 to 
1.0% as on 31 st March, 2007.

reach and serve the rural masses even where they do  not have any physical presence by

525. DR. V. MAITREYAN: Will the Minister of FINANCE be pleased to state:  
the total outstanding loans under various categories which are due for more than three years 
in various Public-Sector Banks; 
the reasons for the huge outstanding; 
the steps being taken to recover these loans; 
whether it is a fact that many banks are writing of f these loans as bad debts causing huge 
losses to the banks vis-a-vis their performances; and 
if so, the reasons for writing off these loans? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRIP AWAN 
KUMAR BANSAL ): (a) As on 31.03.2007, public sector banks (PSBs)  had gross Non-
performing Assets (NPAs) amounting to Rs. 38,974 cr ore, out of which Rs. 14,275 crore 
were in Substandard Assets Category, Rs. 19,873 crore in Doubtful Assets Category and Rs. 
4,826 crore in Loss Assets Category. In percentage terms, these constituted 2.7% (gross 
NPAs), 1.0% (Sub-standard Assets), 1.4% (Doubtful A ssets) and 0.3% (Loss Assets) of 
the total advances of these banks.  
(b) and (c) The factors responsible for NPAs, inter-alia, include diversion of funds by the 
borrower and wilful default in repayment, deficienc y in credit appraisal and supervision, 
inefficient management of the unit financed, poor follow up and monitoring, unviability or 
sickness of the unit due to change in technology demand pattern and other policy etc.m non-
completion of project due to cost and time overruns and other factors, such as non-availability 
of raw materials etc., labour problems, natural cal amities, delay in disposal by courts of 
suits filed by banks, etc. However, the banks monitor their loan accounts at various levels 
and take appropriate corrective action, on an ongoi ng basis, to arrest slippages to NPA 
category.  
Reserve Bank of India (RBI) and the Government of I ndia have taken various steps to 
improve asset quality of the banks which, inter-alia, include prescribing prudential norms 
for provisioning and classification of non-performi ng assets, guidelines for prevention of 
slippages, introduction of Corporate Debt Restructuring mechanism, One Time Settlement 
schemes, enactment of (i) The Securitisation and Re construction of Financial Assets and 
Enforcement of Security Interest (SARFAESI) Act, 2002, (ii) the Credit Information Compa-
nies (Regulation) Act, 2005, and (iii) the Recovery  of Debts due to Banks and Financial 
Institutions (DRT) Act, 1993, etc. Due to concerted efforts, the net NPAs of the PSBs have 
reduced from 4.5% of Net Advances as on 31 st March, 2003 to 1.1 % as on 31 st March, 2007.  
(d)and(e) The banks write-off NPAs for several reasons viz. to cleanse their balance sheets 
through prudential write-offs, to improve asset quality and to get rid of unrealisable portion of 
their bad loans in accordance with their Board approved policies and RBI  guidelines.

Difficulties of LPG consumers  
577.  SHRI RAJNITI PRASAD : Will the Minister of PETROLEUM AND NATURAL 
GAS  
be pleased to state:  
whether Government is aware that there is acute sho rtage of domestic LPG in many parts 
of North India and specially in Bihar; 
whether it is also a fact that the consumers are fa cing serious problems, and they are 
compelled to buy the cylinders from black market at a very high price; 
whether there is an undeclared ban on issue of new gas connections and people are fcrced 
to buy hot-plates from the dealers; and 
the steps being taken by Government to mitigate the problems of poor people and stop black 
marketing by dealers? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTER OF PETROLEUM AND NATURAL 
GAS (SHRI DINSHA J. PATEL ): (a) and (b) Public Sector Oil Marketing Companie s 
(OMCs) have reported that at present, there is no overall shortage of LPG in the country and 
LPG supplies to distributors are being made by the OMCs through indigenous production 
and imports in accordance with the genuine demand of customers registered with the LPG 
distributors. OMCs have further reported that they have supplied 8450 TMT (Thousand 
Metric Tonnes) and 218 TMT of domestic LPG in the c ountry and in State of Bihar 
respectively during the period—April, 2007—January,  2008 as against 8030 TMT and 207 
TMT respectively during the corresponding period of last year.  
However, OMCs had reported backlog in LPG supplies in certain States in the country 
due to reduction in supply of bulk LPG by Reliance Industries Limited (RIL) & Essar Oil 
Limited in January 2008, delay in movement of bulk LPG by rail from Jamnagar to the 
Northern Region, increased demand in the States due to severe cold which resulted in panic  

Written Answers to  [4 MARCH 2008]  Unstarred Questions   117  
booking by the customers, strickes by contract labour, agitational activities, delays in berthing 
of vessels at Haldia Port due to reduced draft, bandhs etc.  
Government has advised OMCs to liquidate the backlo g in the States by operating the 
bottling plants on holidays and during extended hours. Increased bottling is also being done 
during the working days for early clearance of backlog.  
(c) The enrolment of new LPG customers and release of new LPG connections is a 
continuous process. Public Sector Oil Martketing Companies (OMCs) have reported that at 
present, new LPG connections are available across t he counter for genuine domestic cus-
tomers on verification of documents as per laid down procedure.  
OMCs have reported that as on 1.2.2008 they are hav ing 992.9 lakh and 23.8 lakh of 
domestic LPG connections in the country and in the State of Bihar respectively. OMCs have 
also released 1.4 lakh new LPG connections in the S tate of Bihar during the period April, 
2007-January, 2008 as against 0.8 lakh connections during the corresponding period of last  
year.  
OMCs have not directed their LPG distributors to se ll hot-plates of particular compa-
nies for domestic use to customers. However OMCs ha ve tied up with some stove manu-
facturers for production of "Green Label" stoves, w hich have higher thermal efficiency 
and, apart from being economical to the consumers, also, help in conserving fuel and 
protecting the environment. Customsers can purchase these products at competitive prices 
but they are not under any compulsion to purchase the same from the LPG distributors. In 
fact, customers are at liberty to buy these applian ces (meeting BIS specifications) from 
any source of their choice.  
(d) The possibility of black marketing of subsidize d domestic LPG cylinders by some 
unscrupulors elements cannot be ruled out due to th e wide gap between the retail price of 
LPG for domestic use and the market price for commercial LPG  
In order to stop black marketing of LPG cylinders, the Governent has enacted "Liquefied 
Petroleum Gas (Regulation of Supply and Distribution) Order, 2000" and formulated "Mar-
keting Discipline Guidelines, 2001" which provides for penal action against LPG distributors 
indulging in black marketing of LPG  
Whenever OMCs receive complaints, these are investigated and if the complaint is estab-
lished, suitable action is taken against the LPG distributor(s) in accordance with the provi-
sions of the MDG. MDG provides for following action against the distributor-Fine of Rs. 
20,000 plus the price of LPG diverted at commercial rates for 1 st offence. Fine of Rs. 50,000 
plus the price of LPG diverted at commercial rates for 2nd offence. Termination of the 
distributorship for 3rd offence.  
In addition to the action taken by the OMCs, State Governments are empowered under 
the LPG (Regulation of Supply & Distribution) Order, 2000 promulgated under the Essential 
Commodities Act, 1955 to take action against black marketing of domestic LPG Similarly, the 
Weights and Measures Department of the States/UTs i nitiates legal action against those 
LPG distributors found supplying under-weight LPG cylinders. The State Governments have 
been alerted from time to time to take steps against the black-marketing/diversion of domestic 
cylinders for unauthorized usage.

Government have issued advertisments cautioning the public that use of domestic LPG 
for non-domestic purposes is illegal, dangerous and  against national interest. Through 
these advertisements, cooperation of the general public has also been sought to report any 
irregularity/malpractice to the OMCs.  
Further, LPG distributors are also under instructions to ensure 100% weighment of cylin-
ders at their godown before delivery at the custome rs' premises. In a bid to enhance cus-
tomer satisafaction levels, distributors in selected markets have been advised by OMCs to 
provide a spring balance to enable the customers to verify the correctness of the weights of 
LPG in the cylinders. OMCs have introduced this scheme in major markets of the country.  
The officials of OMCs carry out random checks at distributors, godowns, delivery points, 
as well as en-route to ensure that no pilferage tak es place. The distributors of OMCs are 
under strict instruction to check the weight of cyl inder at their godowns before delievery, 
and only cylinders with the specified weight are to  be delivered to the customers. The 
distributors have also been instructed to ensure that the seals are verified and shown to the 
customers at the time of delivery. In case any unde r-weight cylinder is received by the 
customer, such cylinders are replaced with a fresh refill cylinder without any charges levied 
by the OMCs.

Salient features of the Seventh Round of New Exploration Licensing Policy 
(NELP- VII) 
in vogue are as under:

period.

• No mandatory state participation. 
• No carried interest by National Oil Companies (NOC s).

• No customs duty on imports required for petroleum operations. 
• Biddable cost recovery limit: Upto 100%.

pre-tax investment multiple achieved by the contractor.

areas (beyond 400 m iso-bath) royalty is payable fo r both crude oil and 
natural gas at the rate of 5% for the first seven y ears of commercial 
production and thereafter at the rate of 10%. 
• Fiscal stability provision in the contract. 
Freedom to the contractor for marketing of oil and gas in the domestic 
market. 
• Liberal provisions for assignment. 
• Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, based on U nited National

590. DR. V. MAITREYAN:  Will the Minister of PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS  
be pleased to state:  
whether it is a fact that petroleum products are a huge source of drainage of foreign 
exchange as well as severe polluting agent in the country; 
if so, what steps are being taken to identify alter nate source of non-polluting fuel for the 
vehicles in the country; 
whether Government has intensified the R&D work in this area; and 
if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PETROLEUM AND 
NATURALGAS (SHRI DINSHA J. PATEL ): (a) In 2006-07, net expenditure of foreign 
exchange equivalent to US$ 39.6 billion was made in trade of petroleum products. During this 
period, US$ 48.4 billion were spent on the import of crude oil.  
(b) to (d) As efforts to suplement the consumption of petroleum products particularly for 
vehicular application and also to curb emissions, r esearch has been carried out by the 
Ministry of New and Renewable Energy (MNRE) to expl ore the possibility of utilizing 
alternatives for supplementing petrol and diesel. B io-fuels namely, bio-ethanol and bio-
diesel, hydrogen energy and battery operated vehicl es have been identified as potential 
future alternatives to supplement petrol and diesel.  
In the area of Bio-fuels, Ethanol-Gasoline fuels having 5% ethanol content is being used 
in 20 States and 4 Union Territories. Government ha s plans to introduce 10% ethanol in 
States where 5% ethanol is already being used. But vehicle manufacturers are asking for 
more time so as to study the effects of ethanol on material compatibility of in use vehicles.  
 

Written Answers to  [4 MARCH 2008]  Unstarred Questions    131  
IOC R&D and SIAM have been advised to study the effect of 10% ethanol in gasoline on 
various type of in use vehicles.  
Besides spearheading commercialization of ethanol-blended gasoline in the country, Indian 
Oil has been in the fore front of technology develo pment for bio-diesel production from 
various edible/non-edible oils and its application in vehicles.  
Studies by Indian Oil's R&D Centre have established  that bio-diesel produced from 
Jatropha seeds was at par with bio-diesel produced from vegetable oils. In the past few 
years, the Indian Oil R&D Centre has studied the en tire value chain of bio-diesel, starting 
from Jatropha plantation to field trials on passeng er cars, light commercial vehicles and 
railway locos in collaboration with several vehicle manafucturers, Railways and State transpert 
undertakings.  
Homogenous Catalysed Single pot process has also be en developed for production of 
bio-diesel.  
India's first experimental hydrogen-CNG dispensing station was commissioned in the 
campus of IOC R&D at Faridabad and demonstration pr ojects are underway on use of 
Hydrogen-CNG blends in heavy and light vehicles. These projects are funded by Ministry of 
Petroleum and Natural Gas and National Hydrogen Energy Board (NHEB) under Ministry of 
New and Renewable Energy (MNRE) of the Government o f India.  
NHEB under MNRE has estimated about one million veh icles using pure hydrogen or 
hydrogen CNG blended fuel by 2020.

591 . SHRI ABU ASIM AZMI : Will the Minister of PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PETROLEUM AND NATURAL 
GAS (SHRI DINSHA J. PATEL ): (a) to (d) The global prices of crude oil and pe troleum 
products have remained high and volatile since 2004. In view of this, the Public Sector Oil 
Marketing Companies (OMCs) are incurring under-recoveries on domestic sale of sensitive 
petroleum products namely petrol, diesel, PDS kerosene and domestic LPG As passing on 
the entire impact of the steep increase in the oil prices to the consumers would have 
resulted in hardship to the common man, the retail selling prices of petrol, diesel, PDS 
Kerosene and domestic LPG have not been increased i n tandem with the international oil 
prices.  
To meet the escalation in international oil prices, the Government has adopted the principle 
of'equitable burden-sharing' between the Government, the oil PSUs and consumers to protect 
the interests of the common man, vulnerable sections of society and also the financial health 
of OMCs. In this context, the Government has made a marginal increase in petrol and diesel

Statement  
STAND OF MINISTRY OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS :- 
[I]. That the Prior approval of the M/o Environment & Forests [Central Government] is 
required under the Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980 to carry out any non-forestry activity on 
forest land (including the area as per the widened meaning given to word 'forest' by this 
Hon'ble Court in order dated 12.12.1996 in WP(C) No. 202 of 1995 in so far as applicability of 
the Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980 is concerned).  

156    Written Answers to  [RAJYA SABHA]  Unstarred Questions  
[II]. That this Hon'ble Court, vide order dated 14.02.2000 in Writ Petition (C) No. 202 of 
1995, has banned any non-forestry activity within any National Park/Sanctuary, hence, if the 
area on which non-forestry activity is to be carried out falls within any National Park/Sanctuary, 
prior approval of this Hon'ble Court and the National Board for Wildlife is required before the 
proposal can be considered by the Central Government under the Forest (Conservation) Act, 
1980.  
[III]. According to the Guidelines issued under the  Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980, 
which is contained in para 4.4 of the Handbook of Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980 issued by 
the Ministry by Ministry of Environment & Forests, some projects involve use of forest 
Land as well as non-forest land. The State Government/project authorities sometimes start 
work on non-forest lands in anticipation of the app roval of the Central Government for 
release of the forest lands required for the projec ts. Though the provisions of the Act may 
not have technically been violated by starting of w ork on non-forest lands, expenditure 
incurred on works on non-forest lands may prove to be infructuous if diversion of forest land 
involved is not approved. Hence, if a project involves forest as well as non-forest land, work 
should not be started on non-forest land till approval of the Central Government for release 
of forest land under the Forest (Consevation) Act, 1980 has been given'.  
STAND OF PLANNING COMMISSION , WATER RESOURCES DIVISION :- 
"Planning Commission guidelines for according investment clearance (Dated 30.11.2000) 
clearly stipulates that" any project which is located in an Inter State river or its tributary will 
be deemed to involve interstate remification and as  such need investment clearance from 
Planning Commission". The Planning Commission's guidelines requiring clearance for change 
of water use pattern in an inter-state river or its tributary is subject to technical appraisal by 
a competent agency such a Central Water Commission. If the Planning Commission's guideline 
is now deemed to apply only for projects where Plan funds (Centre or State) are being used, 
then the guidelines can be circumvented by saying t hat the funds used will be non-Plan. 
This interpretation is too flexible. The spirit of the guidelines is that Inter-State water use 
pattern cannot be changed without approval irrespec tive of whether Plan or Non-Plan 
resources are used.

Irrigation Benefit Programme in Rajasthan  
621. DR. GYAN PRAKASH PILANIA: Will the Minister of WATER RESOURCES be 
pleased to state:  
 
what were the projects taken up during the Tenth Five Year Plan period, under the 
Accelerated Irrigation Benefit Programme in Rajasthan; 
how many were completed and what was the irrigation potential targeted and actually created 
during plan period; 
what was cost escalation, due to delay, project-wise; 
what is the allocation during Eleventh Plan; 
what is Government's reaction to the pace of implementation; and 
the steps being taken to complete the projects on time? 

160    Written Answers to  [RAJYA SABHA]  Unstarred Questions  
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER RESO URCES 
(SHRI JAI PRAKASH NARAYAN YADAV ): (a) to (c) No new project of Rajasthan was 
taken up during the 10th Plan under Accelerated Irrigation Benefits Programme (AIBP). Seven 
Major/Medium/ Extension, Renovation and Modernisation (ERM) Projects of Rajasthan were 
considered for Central Assistance (CA) under Accele rated Irrigation Benefit Programme 
(AIBP) during 10th Plan, out of which 4 projects ha ve been completed. The names and 
irrigation potential targeted/achieved of these sev en projects are given in the Statement 
(See below). No price escalation in Modernisation of Gan g Canal has been reported 
whereas cost escalation in Indira Gandhi Nahar Pari yojana (IGNP) Stage-II and Narmada 
Canal is mainly due to change in scope. The revised  scope of Narmada Canal has been 
approved by the Planning Commission.  
(d) to (f) The 11th Plan outlay for AIBP is Rs. 39850 crore. State- wise annual AIBP ceiling 
for each State is finalized by the Planning Commission based on State Plan discussions and 
progress of the works. On the basis of reviews and monitoring done from time to time, the 
Ministry of Water Resources has initiated several measures to expedite completion of ongoing 
irrigation projects under AIBP which includes vigorous monitoring of the projects, linking 
utilization of Central Assistance to physical achie vements in terms of potential creation, 
release of grants based on Memorandum of Understand ing and Utilization Certificates, 
taking up new projects only against completion of one ongoing project etc.

Motion of Thanks  [4 MARCH 2008]  on President's Address   175  
SHRI R.K. DHAWAN (Bihar): Mr. Deputy Chairman, Sir, with your permission, I rise to 
support the Motion of Thanks to the hon. President's Address. Sir, at the outset, I would like 
to thank the hon. President for her illuminating ad dress to Parliament. Sir, as this august 
House knows, the President's Address is a statement made on behalf of the Government; the 
Address represents, generally, the programmes and policies of the Government. It is not a 
catalogue of what all the Government has done. It i s a concise statement in the restrained 
language which gives the details, because it is not  possible to give all the details that the 
Government wishes to give, if I may say so. My colleague Janardhan Dwivediji has made a 
very lucid analysis of the programmes and policies of the Government and Shri Singhviji has 
quoted various figures. I would not like to take the time of the hon. House in repeating all 
that. However, I would like to say a few words on some subjects, primarily on agriculture.  
Sir, the Congress Party fought the 2004 elections on the philosophy that the objective of 
any Government is not the glory of the rulers but the happiness of the common man. I have 
no hesitation in saying, much to the discomfort of my friends in the Opposition, that this has 
been the major factor for the Government in framing policies and programmes, to be responsible 
and transparent on all counts, and the Government has achieved many strides.  
Last year, while speaking on the same Motion, I emphasised the importance of having a 
second Green Revolution. Sir, it is a matter of great exhilaration for me that the Government 
during the last one year has made tremendous progre ss towards attainment of this 
indispensable national objective. Sir, it is hearte ning to note from the Address that the 
National Food Security Mission has been set up to e nhance the production of rice, wheat 
and pulses by 10, 8 and 2 million tonnes during the  Eleventh Plan period. Sir, another 
praiseworthy action taken by the Government is Rashtriya Krishi Vikas Yojana with an outlay 
of Rs.25,000 crores for farmers revival by setting up agriculture growth of 4 per cent in the 
Eleventh Plan by providing incentives to States. Sir, for understanding the need of Second 
Green Revolution to which our Bhandaryji also referred, one has to go back into the history 
of development of agriculture since Independence. Sir, when this country became independent, 
Shri Jawaharlal Nehru, the first Prime Minister, had the vision and foresight that India had to 
catch up with the rest of the world in the field of  industrial development and without 
industrialisation economic growth will not be able to match the world. With that in mind, he 
set up public sector undertakings to have industrial infrastructure and took initiative for the 
private sector to grow. Sir, but for historical experiences India had gone through, it was not 
possible to regulate, it was not possible to allow private sector to have the growth in its own 
manner because of the limitation of resources at th at time, much investment could not be 
made in the agricultural sector and result was the country in the sixties' had to face a very 
difficult situation so far as wheat was concerned a nd had to depend on import of wheat to 
save the millions of people from starvation. Sir, w hen Mrs. Gandhi took over the reins of 
office, and I am a witness to those events from 1966 onwards, she felt that economic progress 
would be an illusion only until and unless we becom e self-sufficient in the production of 
food and agricultural products. So, this was the vi sion that Mrs. Gandhi took and the 
initiative she took to have the Green Revolution and the manner in which production grew in 
few years, India got self-sufficiency in food is ma tter of record that is for nobody else to 
dispute. Sir, I have got no doubt in my mind that the gigantic step that the Government has 
taken in the field of agriculture will be the harbinger of Second Green Revolution in India. Sir, 

176 Motion of Thanks  [RAJYA SABHA]  on President's Address  
the country has made tremendous economic progress, economic growth has been the 
phenomenon. But unless fruit and benefits of this economic growth reach the millions of people 
who toil and sweat in the fields to serve the country, it will be only a matter of speech. So, something 
has to be done about that to improve the lot of the farmers for which this UPA Government is totally 
committed. Sir, I feel gratified to the UPA Government that it is fully alive to the problems, needs, 
and predicaments of the farmers. It is no ordinary achievement that the Government has effected an 
unprecedented growth, steep hike of 50 per cent in the Minimum Support Price of wheat and 33 per 
cent for paddy in the last four years. There is no denying the fact that for better marketing facilities,

[4 MARCH 2008]  on President's Address    191  
Sir, coming to the Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and OBCs, the President's Address 
says that they are extending financial assistance to them. I demand that you come out with 
a white paper as to what are the details. In view of the larger Budget and outlays, the money 
allocated to the Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and OBCs is very meagre. Sir, I have got 
an answer from the hon. Minister yesterday. I am holding it. Sir, the reservation for SCs, STs 
and OBCs in judiciary is not there. The answer says  that they need a constitutional 
amendment. Why don't you come out with that? The Parliamentary Standing Committee on 
Personnel, Public Grievances and Pension, Law and Justice has given a detailed report on 
this aspect. I demand that there should be a constitutional amendment to help the SCs, STs 
and OBCs to have reservations in the judiciary.  
Sir, coming to essential commodities, the NCMP and the President's Address speaks 
about aam admi. But, they have forgotten about the essential commodities and rising prices. 
Aam admi is not in a position to purchase them. Having raise d the prices of petroleum 
products seven times, it has got multiplier effect on aam admi. Sir, I demand that the 
Government should take concrete steps in containing  the prices of essential commodities; 
otherwise, it's going to be a very big problem for the rural poor. _Sir, coming to the health 
sector, thereport says that there are some flagship  programmes like National Rural Health 
Mission and Bharat Nirman. All those phrases are good, but in reality, people are forced to go 
for private treatment, and all the primary health centres have become defunct. There are no 
doctors in rural areas, no medical facilities are available and people are forced to go to the 
private hospitals by paying higher prices. They are not in a position to afford these medical 
expenses. Sir, the hon. Health Minister, while introducing the National Rural Health Mission 
programme, and that was also mentioned in the President's Address, referred to ASHA. For 
everything, they say that ASHA is in place. Sir, for everything, ASHA! I don't understand 
this. Sir, I come from the rural area. I was also a sarpanch of the village. I know the practical 
difficulties in this. Ultimately, this ASHA program me is going to end up in nirasha. For 
everything, they are depending on ASHA. They are not fully equipped, they are not experts 
in medical field, they will only assist the people. But, where are the doctors? Where is the 
facility? Where is the infrastructure? So, all these things need attention.  
Coming to education, very high appreciation is placed on record by the hon. President. I 
would like to refer to the Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan. A s announced yesterday in this august 
House, a lot of money diverted is misused, is misappropriated. In the answer, the CAG report 
for 2005-06 says, the money involved is Rs. 6.8 crores in Assam, Rs. 15.8 crores in Bihar, Rs. 
22.9 crores in Gujarat, Rs. 4.7 crores in Karnataka and Rs. 15 crores in Andhra Pradesh. In 
Andhra Pradesh, in this scam, one officer who is working in the hon. Chief Minister's office, 
is himself involved. The Government of India is not  at all taking any concrete steps in 
recovering the money, in booking the culprits so as  to save the money and help the poor 
people for whom we are paying cess to the Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan programme. I would like 
to demand a total inquiry into this scam. For the Mid-day Meals scheme also, the infrastructure 
is inadequate. Infrastructure like kitchen shed, st orage room, plates, glasses, utensils, all 
these things are not at all put in place. I request  the Government of India to help the State 
Governments to help the school committees in upgrading the present infrastructure.  
Coming to the other infrastructure like roads, the condition of rural roads is very bad 
except the Golden Quadrilateral roads, north-south corridor, east-west corridor and other 
programmes, the rural areas roads are totally neglected, and in the Bharat Nirman programme, 
it is mentioned that roads are improved and a lot of money is spent on that. Practically,  

192 Motion of Thanks  [RAJYA SABHA]  on President's Address  
nothing is happening on the rural roads. I would request the Government to concentrate on 
these things.  
Under the National Rural Employment Guarantee programme, they have given promise to 
the nation through their NCMP. I would read out the opening sentence of this NCMP. They 
said: The UPA Government will immediately enact a National Rural Employment Guarantee 
Act. This will provide a legal guarantee for, at least 100 days of employment. In the initial 
stage, they have introduced it for 150 districts. Thereafter, it is made into 300 districts. Now, 
at the fag end of their tenure, they say that it is going to be implemented for the entire nation. 
I would like to caution the Government on this count that there are reports from the special 
audit and they are not placed before the people. Th ey should be made public. The social 
audit reports say that a lot of misuse is taking place, and the job cards which are meant for the 
poor workers, now have become ATM cards for the Congress party workers. They can draw 
money any time. For the convenience of the Congress  party workers, this programme has 
become a Congress Party Workers Employment Programme, not for the common poor people, 
who are really in distress in the rural areas. I ha ve an instance. I have the record with me 
wherein, in the name of a dead person, money is dra wn. A lot of reports are there from 
districts like Anantapur, Cuddapah and Mahbubnagar of my own State, where the hon. Prime 
Minister launched the Programme. There is a total m isuse, Sir. And the people who went 
there for social audit were not allowed to enter the village; they were locked up in the room. 
This is the state of affairs as far as the National Rural Employment Guarantee Programme is 
concerned. I would like the Government to have a total review of the Programme and book 
the culprits.  
Women reservation, as my earlier speakers mentioned about it, my party is committed to 
this, and we have been demanding one-third reservation for women. This was promised in 
the NCMP: "The UPA Government will take lead to int roduce a legislation for one-third 
reservation for women in Vidhan Sabhas and Lok Sabh a." Sir, nothing is happening; not 
even the introduction of the Bill. No concrete steps have been taken in this regard. Just for 
sake of their votes, they are saying that they are interested in one-third reservation for 
women. A legislation should immediately be brought to this august House and should also 
be passed.  
I come to the Reports which are pending with the Go vernment. For example, there are 
Reports like the Swaminathan Commission Report—that  was submitted in October, 2006— 
Sachar Committee Report and Arjun Sengupta Commission Report which are pending with 
the Government. So many Reports are there with the Government, but the Government is not 
at all implementing them. They are just lying over there. I demand that those Reports should 
be placed before the House; there should be a discussion, and they should be implemented 
in toto. Otherwise, the very purpose of constituting those Committees will be defeated.  
Coming to the Indo-U.S. nuclear deal, again, the hon. President has stressed on the Indo-
U.S. nuclear deal. We oppose the deal. It is a thre at to our sovereignty. And the amount 
involved is Rs.3,30,000 crores. This money will go only to private companies and a few 
individuals. Otherwise, our people are deprived of roads, health, education, and everything. 
When we are in a position to generate one megawatt of power with Rs.4 crores, why should 
we pay Rs.ll crores for one megawatt though this In do-U.S. nuclear deal? We fail to 
understand that. We demand that the deal should be stopped. Otherwise, it is going to be a 
threat to the sovereignty of our nation.  
Coming to para 35 wherein the hon. President has me ntioned about the coming up of 

Motion of Thanks                  [4 MARCH 2008]  on President's Address   I93  
airports in Hyderabad and Bangalore, Sir, these airports were conceived, contemplated and started 
during the previous dispensation, and my leader, Mr. Chandrababu Naidu, was in the forefront in 
getting mis Greenfield Airport to Hyderabad. They are going to inaugurate the Hyderabad Airport on 
March 14, this month only. Who is inaugurating? Not the President; not the P.M. An M.P. from Uttar 
Pradesh is going over there to inaugurate! How she is entitled, I don't understand. They are going to 
create a very bad precedent. What is her capacity? Sir, we object to this, and at the same time, we 
also object to the naming of the airport They are closing the Begumpet Airport, which was called the 
Rajiv Gandhi International Airport, with an N.T. Rama Rao domestic terminal. Now, they are going to 
shift the entire airport on March 14, and they are naming in only after Shri Rajiv Gandhi while ignoring 
the name of Shri N.T. Rama Rao. Sir, we object to this. The Government of India is habituated; the present 
dispensation is habituated in changing the names of great people like Shri N.T. Rama Rao. To this, we 
take strong objection, and the Government should definitely amend it and take steps for mat; 
otherwise this is going to be a big problem.  
Sir, coming to other aspects like infrastructure and irrigation, recently, the Government of India has 
given a lot of money for 14 irrigation projects as national projects, but not for even one project in 
Andhra Pradesh. The southern States are totally neg lected. And in case of sanctioning other 
institutions, Central Universities and everything, Andhra Pradesh is neglected. I demand that there 
should be a reasonable distribution of institutions, a reasonable distribution of assets to Southern 
India.  
With these words, I oppose the Motion. Thank you, Sir.  
THE VICE-CHAIRMAN (SHRI DINESH TRIVEDI): Thank you, Shri Reddy.

DR. P.CALEXANDER (Maharashtra): Mr. Vice-Chairman, Sir, I thank you for giving me 
an opportunity to participate in the discussions on the Motion of Thanks to the President's 
Address. I am conscious of the fact that this is the last opportunity for me to participate in a 
discussion the President's Address because in a ver y short time I will be completing my 
tenure in this House.  
I mention this because I wfeuld like to raise a few basic issues regarding the functioning of 
our democracy and share with you some of my concern s about the directions that our 
democracy has taken in recent years. I will be basing my speech mainly on the observations 
made by the President in her speech on three points . And my fourth point will be on a 
conspicuous omission that I wish to point out in the President's Speech.  
My first point, Sir, is concerning the last paragraph of the President's Speech which gives 
a ringing exhortation to the people of this country about the functioning of democracy in our 
country. I quote this sentence. It is a very inspiring sentence. It says, "Therefore, what you 
say and do in these hallowed portals of democracy will have a bearing not just on the destiny 
of our people, but also on the future of democracy and free societies around the world."  
Sir, the question that I wish to raise before the h on. House is this. Is this assumption 
about the health of our democracy really justifiable? We are implementing the parliamentary 
system of democracy for the last 60 years. The foundations for this system were truly laid by 
the greatest democrat of that time, not the greates t democrat of India, but the greatest 
democrat of that time, Pandit Jawaharlal Nehru. By the time he finished his 18 years of 
stewardship of the State, people had begun to feel confident that our democracy was on 
proper lines. But if we now look at the direction our democracy has taken and the manner in 
which it is functioning in our country, I feel genuinely concerned whether we will last as a 
democracy for a long time. The basic principle of Parliamentary democracy is that it has to be 
founded on a sound and healthy party system. Some o ther systems of Government can be 
practised without reference to political parties, b ut the Parliamentary system can function 
only if you have a good, healthy and sound party system in the country. Let us ask ourselves 
this question honestly. Do we have a good party system in this country? At any rate taking 
into account the manner in which parties are functi oning today, can we call that really 
healthy? Or, have we distorted the basic concepts o f democracy in the working of our 
parties? How can we think of having a healthy democracy at the Government level, if at the 
party level we do not practise democracy? It is unt hinkable because it is a contradiction to 
have democracy being implemented by political parti es which do not practise democracy 
within the parties. I am concerned, Sir, at the trend that has set in today, by which parties are 
run without any elections. The people seem to have forgotten that the functionaries of the 
parties have to be elected according to the will of the party members. But we have converted 
elections into nominations. And, the culture that is prevailing in most political parties, with 
the exception of three, or, four, which I do not want to name today, is the nomination culture 
masquerading as elections. It is all settled somewhere as to who is to be the President of the 
State party, who is to be the convenor of this, or,  the chairman of that, and, then, there are 
supposed to have been approved by the people through elections. This will eat into the  

Motion of Thanks  [4 MARCH 2008]  on President's Address   203  
vitals of the political system in our country. After some time, a whole generation will grow up 
thinking that this is how party system should be do ne, and, then, our democracy will get 
completely devalued. Sir, this is a warning signal that I am raising, after deep study and full 
sense of responsibility. When the Freedom House con ducted a survey of 193 countries of 
the world, they listed only 90 countries as democracy; they had listed 60 countries as partly 
democratic and the rest has non democratic. India has been included in the 90 countries. But 
if the present trend, continues for some more years, of dispensing with elections at the party 
level, depending entirely on nominations, we will very soon get into the category of partly-
democratic countries. And, God knows what will happen then. The way the Parties are being 
run by individuals would really be a matter of envy for the great dictators of the world. That 
generation dictators has gone. They also called the mselves democratic and we looked at 
them with contempt; but this is the way our Parties are being run today. Certain individuals 
run the parties as it God has given them the wisdom and the right to do so and we call that 
democracy. If we continue this trend, we will not b e justified in claiming that the world 
outside will be looking to us for inspiration and our democracy will be having greater lustre 
and eminence.  
The second point connected with the future of democracy I wish to flag on this occasion 
is the devaluation of the institutions of democracy. Sir, how many minutes are given to me?  
THE VICE-CHAIRMAN (PROF. P. J. KURIEN): Fifteen minutes.  
DR. P.C. ALEXANDER: Thank you, Sir. I don't have the time to refer to devaluation of all 
the institutions of democracy. But let me take the devaluation of the institution to which we 
all  belong, namely of the institution of legislature. Sir, among all the institutions of democracy, 
namely, legislature, executive, Civil Service, Judiciary for forces and non-political military 
service, the most important is the one in which we are members, the legislature. Can we 
honestly say, Sir, that the legislatures in our country at the central level and at the State level 
are being run in the manner in which the legislatures should be run?  
Sir, I came to this House six years ago. Looking around the Benches, I could see some of 
the brilliant parliamentarians, some very brilliant minds in this House and I always used to tell 
my friends mat the Rajya Sabha is very rich in talents. On this side and that side and in the 
back Benches of the nominated Members, we find men of outstanding talents. But do you 
give them a chance to participate in debates, to contribute to the working of democracy in 
this hallowed institution? Do we find even the most talented people being able to make their 
contribution effectively in the legislature? Do we discuss the problems which should be 
really worrying us almost day-to-day as the custodians of democracy in this country. Take 
some of these problems. Farmers are committing suicide, not in hundreds but in thousands. 
The Rural Employment Guarantee Scheme is supposed to be the star scheme and I,agree it 
has to be the star scheme for fighting poverty. The re are issues like the corruption in this 
country, the all-pervasive corruption that is eating into the vitals of our nation. Do we get the 
time to discuss any of these issues in depth ? The only debate that I can recall, which has 
been seriously conducted in this House both by the Opposition and by the Government and 
which will stand out as one of the best debates this House has witnessed in the past six years 
that I know of, was the debate on the 'Indo-US Nucl ear Cooperation.' But what about the 
other subjects which are of equal importance to us?  Why are we not spending days to 
consider them, discuss them and why are we not giving freedom to the Government Benches 
to express their views during those discussions? No voting is involved, but still a whip is  

204 Motion of Thanks  [RAJYA SABHA]  on President's Address  
indirectly given to them not to oppose Government p olicies, most unlike the working of 
democratic institutions in western countries. We really have to revise the way we, conduct our 
own business in this House. Otherwise, this institution will get devalued and become a subject of 
ridicule.  
Sir, let me raise another warning signal. The probl ems, which should be worrying us, 
causing us sleepless nights, seem to be completely forgotten and we try to build up our dreams 
and to live in a dream world of our own. We go about telling the people that in twenty years' time or 
now in twelve years' time, India is going to be one of the developed countries of the world. By 
merely making bhasans to people who are not aware of facts and figures that by 2020 India will 
join the ranks of the most developed countries of the world, we are deceiving them and we are 
deceiving ourselves. It is because as I see the situation today, most unlikely, we will — and I say 
again with full sense of confidence and with all humility— reach most unlikely the levels of the 
developed countries of the world even in a hundred years. Sir, the United Nations Development 
Programme Report is very significant. They have put us down at the 128* rank in the countries of 
the world from the point of view of human development based on income, literacy or education and 
healthcare. Our per capita income is one-tenth that of the developed countries. The UNDP Report 
says that even if the developed countries do not add one dollar to their income and remain static and 
India tries to reach that level, it will take one hundred years to reach that level. When that is the 
reality and when we have to face that problem with that reality in mind, we go on telling people 
that within 12 or 20 years from now, we are going to enter into the ranks of the developed 
countries of the world. Selling dreams is easy, Sir. You can win votes for five years but you 
cannot be doing this every fifth year because you will get into trouble. Once the disillusioned 
masses feel the winds of change and feel the winds of what is happening in the country, the 
distortions in the distribution of wealth, they are not going to keep quiet. And then our democracy 
itself would face new problems which may be dangerous for its very existence.  
I now come to strategies for development. Since the time is limited, I would refer to only the 
main strategy that should be relied upon, that is, the Rural Employment Guarantee Act. I have great 
faith in this Act; I have great faith in this scheme. Mr. Manohar Joshi was Chief Minister of 
Maharashtra when I was the Governor of the State. During the ten years that I was Governor of 
Maharashtra, the State had contributed so much to the reduction of unemployment in rural areas 
that they had practically snubbed the edge of poverty, the de-humanising poverty in certain rural 
areas of the country. The Employment Guarantee Sche me, according to the President, is 
expected to soften the sharp edges of poverty and offer basic livelihood and security. Sir, the way 
we have started does not give me any hope; if this scheme is implemented, We may spend Rs. 
20,000 crores, but the number of households helped, the number of unemployed people assisted, 
will be much less than what we have ever bargained for. I will give you one piece of statistics 
which should make us think about the direction in which this scheme has been proceeding. It has 
been seen from the report published by the Ministry that during the year 2006-2007, 2.10 crores 
of households have benefited by the Employment Guarantee Scheme. I request the House to note 
these figures carefully. According to the published report of the Ministry of Rural Development 
during the year 2006-07,2.10 crores of households have benefited from the scheme. But if you go 
deep into the report — not that report but other reports published by the same Ministry — you 
will find that, in the same year, when you claimed that 2.10 crores of households have 
benefited, actually, only 37 days was the average n umber of days when employment was 
provided. While 100 days' employment has been provided for in the Act, only 37 days of  

Motion of Thanks  [4 MARCH 2008]  on President's Address   205  
average employment had been provided during this period. Where are the 100 days? Where are the 
2.10 crores of households said to have benefited by the scheme? Not only that, only 7.59 lakhs of 
households out of the 2.10 crores of benefIcary had received 100 days of employment. This is 
a dismal story. This is not the way that this scheme should have started. If we go at this rate, people 
would lose confidence in that. And, therefore, it i s time that a Parliamentary Committee is 
appointed to give a new direction to this scheme and to ensure that the hopes and aspirations of 
those who introduced this scheme are really fulfilled on proper lines on which this scheme was 
expected to be implemented.  
One simple point that I will mention as a success s tory in Maharashtra. They gave 
practically complete flexibility to the local bodies and to the local officers to decide about 
entitlement and the type of employment to be given and one direction they gave was that they 
can link the Rural Employment Scheme with Horticulture Development Scheme. It was a 
wonderful decision. The result was, Maharashtra which had hardly 173 thousand hectares of 
horticulture in 9 or 10 years, from 1990 to 2000, because of the linkage of the Employment 
Guarantee Scheme with the Horticulture Development Scheme, the number of hectares under 
employment cultivation increased from 117 thousand to 971 thousand hectares and women were 
the greatest beneficiaries. Instead of asking them to dig mud and carry heavy loads on their starved 
heads and bodies, they were doing cultivation, which they like even without assistance, of fruits 
and vegetables and they earn much more man they could. Like that, we could give direction and 
there should be some special committee of the Parliament to give direction. Otherwise, this 
ambitious scheme can go waste. Sir, I now come to the most important point that I wish to make 
and that is with regard to some of the real sad problems of our nation which seem to have escaped 
our attention and concern. We speak of poverty, but the type of poverty mat our people have is 
what Arjun Sengupta has brought out in his Report. I do not know whether he is present here. It is a 
very useful and valuable Report on the unorganised sector in our country and we got that 
astonishing figure that 79 per cent of 395 million workers in the unorganised sector are living with 
Rs.20 a day or less. To keep a cat in our house or to keep a dog in our house, we have to spend, at 
least, Rs.300 or Rs.400 a month, and here we are keeping our own workers, our own flesh and 
blood, calling them workers in the unorganised sector, and allowing them to live within Rs.18 or 
Rs.20 a day. Arjun Sengupta Report has not even been brought before this House. I wonder why it 
is not being discussed in this House. Such a Report should have got top priority over many other 
reports and should have been discussed here. But we have not done it. These are the points that 
arise from the Speech. There is my last point and that is an omission in the Speech. I do not, Sir, 
why there was no mention of it in the Speech. When all other matters have been discussed and 
when a whole catalogue of scheme has been introduced or referred to, why we—those who 
drafted the Speech—have not advised the President to say a paragraph on all pervasive corruption 
that has destroyed all development schemes as is threatening to put us back to where we were 
even 10 years earlier. Sir, to speak about corruption is to invite criticism because people say that 
they have heard the story before or they will say put your search light inside and see whether your 
civil servants are not corrupt or more corrupt than we politicians. Whatever we may say, Sir, the 
unfortunate situation today is mat civil servants, and that to senior civil servants, politicians, 
educationists, and even those who control the temples, mosques and churches are also indulging 
in corruption. And, this corruption is so prevalent that we are all tolerating it as if nothing is of 
consequence in this land of Mahatma Gandhi. It is not only a tragedy but it is a crime. The greatest 
man ever born in this  

206 Motion of Thanh  [RAJYA SABHA]  on President's Address  
world in the 20th Century, Mahatma Gandhi, is great  not because he gave us freedom, others have 
given freedom to their countries; not because he sh owed us a new way of attaining freedom, others 
have followed different course; the greatest claim for his greatness as Mahatma is cleanliness in publ ic 
life, absolute, impeccable, unquestionable integrit y. In his land, if we have descended to this level of 
corruption, no amount of praise for the development  schemes will be of any avail. Therefore, this 
has been a conspicuous omission in the speech. With  these words, I conclude my speech.  
THE VICE-CHAIRMAN (PROF. P.J. KURIEN): Now, Shri Ali Anwar.

[4 MARCH 2008]  on President's Address   229  
THE VICE-CHAIRMAN (PROF. P.J. KURIEN ): Shri Prasanta Chatterjee, your party is 
left with one minute only. But you should conclude in ten minutes. ...(Interruptions)... 
What is left is one minute only, but you can conclude in ten minutes. I am giving you ten 
fold increase.  
SHRI PRASANTA CHATTERJEE  (West Bengal): Sir, I will try and finish my 
speech within the allotted time itself. Yesterday, our leader Comrade Sitaram Yechury 
elaborately recorded the views of CPI(M) on the Presidential Address, and also in the 
context of the Government's claim on economic growth and foreign affairs, particularly, 
on Israel and the Palestinian peoples' rights. I will confine my views to other arenas.  
The views expressed in the speech of the hon. President appear to be one-sided as 
there is no admission of harsh realities. Many important issues affecting the common 
people have not found any place in her Address. How can we deny that every year, 
approximately, rupees one lakh crores are being accumulated as black money? Some 
reports have indicated this.  
Prosperity for the rich and affluent, and deprivations for the majority of people is the 
essence of today's exclusive growth. India's position in the Human Development Index is 
128 out of the total 177 countries while it was 126 last year. And, as per the Global Hunger 
Index, India's position is 94*.  
Sir, the entire country is reeling under unprecedented price rise of every essential 
commodity. Systematic demolition of the entire Public Distribution System has added fuel 
to the fire. The Union Government is slashing down the quota of foodgrains for P.D.S. 
meant for Kerala and West Bengal. Just before the commencement of this Budget Session, 
the Union Government opted for hiking the prices of petrol and diesel for the eighth time, 
without taking the course of lowering down the taxes on fuel. It is obvious that this price 
hike will lead to further rise of prices of all essential commodities.  
In spite of the growth of GDP to the extent of 8.5 per cent, the growth rate in the 
agricultural sector is only 2 per cent. This is a serious issue. Farmers should get agricultural 
inputs at cheaper prices and they should get remunerative prices for their products. Land 
reforms are extremely necessary. For implementation of these necessary steps, political will 
of the Union Government is the pre-condition. Unfortunately, these serious facts have not 
found any place in the Presidential Address.  
Sir, time and again, we expressed our anxiety over the unemployment situation in the  
country. Employment in the public sector has declined from 194 lakhs in 1994 to 182 lakhs  
in 2004. Casualisation of labour, outsourcing and widespread use of contract workers have  
 subjected workers to greater exploitation and deprived them of their rights.  
(Unfortunately, these serious facts too have not found any place in the Presidential Address.  
Sir, the hon. President, in her speech, expressed her pleasure for introduction of 
Unorganised Sector Social Security Bill, 2007. Unfortunately, the Bill is not in consistent 
with the Statement of Objects and Reasons appended with the Bill itself. The Bill contains 
neither a compelling provision regarding the floor level social security nor for the universal 
coverage of all unorganised sector workers. It also does not have a clearly defined funding 
obligation and a time frame.  
The National Commission for Enterprises in the Unorganised Sector, appointed by the 
Union Government, has already presented its report on August 6,2007, to the Prime Minister, 
with its detailed recommendations evolved after elaborate consultations with the Central  

230 Motion of Thanks  [RAJYA  SABHA]  on President's Address  
Trade Unions. The report includes two draft Bills titled "Agricultural Workers' Conditions of Work 
and Security Bill, 2007 and Unorganised Non-Agricultural Workers Social Security Bill, 2007." 
The Government is yet to take a decision on the recommendations made by the Commission set 
up by the UPA Government itself.  
As such, the hon. President should have expressed her displeasure on the attitude of her 
Government towards the unorganised sector workers.  
Sir, I have already mentioned India's position on Human Development Index and also on Global 
Hunger Index. The high incidence of malnutrition, high infant and maternal mortality rate, illiteracy 
etc. are the main reasons behind these shabby conditions. These problems should be addressed 
through ICDS.  
Out of the total Rs. 16.4 crores eligible children, only 6.29 crores are covered by ICDS, as on 
31" December, 2007. The UPA Government is committed to universalize the ICDS in its NCMP. 
The Apex Court directed universalisation of the ICDS by the end of 2008.  
Unfortunately, not a single word on this serious issue, involving mothers and children, has 
found a place in the President's Address.  
Sir, the hon. President, in her speech, has express ed high satisfaction on the issue of 
Special Economic Zone. I do not know whether it is known to hon. President that the workers 
and employees working inside the Special Economic Zones are deprived of almost all labour 
rights, including Trade Union rights.  
Sir, permit me to take up the performances of Indian Railways. The hon. President left no word 
of praise for Indian Railways. According to the hon. President, Indian Railways has achieved a 
major turnaround in the financial performances.  
I beg to be excused by the Chair as well as by the Minister of Railways for my comments 
hereinafter.  
Sir, once upon a time, Railways was the biggest employer in the country. Systematically, Indian 
Railways are privatising its services. In different sectors, railways is surrendering all vacant posts, 
closing the cadre and creating supernumerary posts and freezing the cadres. The railways have 
decided to close all ticket printing presses and general presses by August 1,2009. It has also 
decided to outsource the jobs of printing.  
Sir, I am afraid that hon. Minister for Railways has forgotten his own statement made on 10* 
September, 2004. On that day, in his address to a two-day conference of the General Managers 
of the Zonal Railways, the production units and the Kolkata Metro in Delhi, the hon. Minister for 
Railways said that he would rather quit than allow privatization, as the private sector would not 
meet the aspirations of the people. Making a total U-turn, the Railways have given an 
unprecedented emphasis on Special Purpose Vehicle, Public-Private partnership and Build-Operate-
Transfer in wide areas of activities, from cleaning of coaches, building of flyovers, wagon 
ownership and management to gradually increased participation in infrastructure development.  
Unfortunately, the President's speech has failed to  address the important issues of 
continuous downsizing in Railways and outsourcing perennial nature of jobs in the name of 
public-private participation.  
Sir, the Communal Violence Bill is still pending. The Standing Committee submitted its 
Report last year. This Bill has not come up as yet in the Parliament for discussion. The hon. Home 
Minister is here. I demand that this Bill should come up for discussion in the House  

Motion of Thanks  [4 MARCH 2008]  on President's Address   231  
immediately.  The issue of compensation for the victims was also deal there. The hon. 
Members from the Left Parties in the Standing Committee have given their comments.  
Sir, my Party, alongwith the Left Parties, is rendering its support to the UPA Government 
on the basis of the National Common Minimum Programme. Time and again, we have 
cautioned the Government and demanded strict adherence to the NCMP. The Government 
should make an introspection of its performances, accept the realities and take corrective 
steps. With these few words, I conclude. Thank you.

SHRI ARJUN KUMAR SENGUPTA: This is the simple finding that if we really want to have 
'inclusive growth', we cannot depend only on a high rate of economic growth. We did not talk 
about the period after 2004-05. 1 must mention this because a reference has been made to this 
report by different party leaders as if this report was against the current Government. It is 
nothing of that sort. Sir, the year 2004-05 is the last number which you have used. After that, a 
number of things have happened which we are discussing now, but our report is basically for the 
nineties period of high rate of economic growth. Mr. Vice-Chairman, I want to put forward that 
our report is completely non-partisan. Of those ten years, only the first few years were ruled by 
the Congress. The reforms process was initiated by Dr. Manmohan Singh and that has fruitioned 
into a very high rate of growth. But during that period, we had also the United Front Government, of 
which Shri Chidambaram was the Finance Minister. Two Communist leaders were members of 
that Government. They supported the policies of economic reforms. After that, it was the 
NDA, the BJP Government, which ran the show. So, this is not a partisan report. All the parties 
were involved. Now the time has come to introspect. What has happened? Why was it that the 
high rate of growth did not translate into a robust inclusive growth? That is the only question 
that we ask and we try to formulate some answers to that.  
We have analysed the earlier periods of Nehruji; I do not want to talk about Indiraji's period. 
The only point I wanted to mention was that although the rate of growth during this period was 
only 3.75 to 4 per cent, this was three times the rate of growth of the previous thirty years. And 
during this period, we built up our capacity, built up our skills and built up our high industrial 
structure. All these things happened. But that is not the purpose of our report. The purpose of our 
report was very simple: how to have this inclusive growth?  
Sir, the most important finding that we have is that if we want to have inclusive growth, then 
the growth arid the policies related to growth must be targeted to the poorest of the poor. For 
that, we have to identify the small and marginal farmers, the unorganised workers, the very small 
enterprises which are employing less than ten units and having a capital of less than Rs. 25 lakhs. 
These are the people who are at the lowest rung of our total population. If I may say so, it also 
shows that this is the group to which most of the Muslims, most of the Dalits and most of die 
OBCs belong. So, it is a congruence of income pover ty, social poverty and all kinds of 
deprivation. And they have to be looked after. If y ou want mat inclusive growth, the policy 
should orient towards that. And the most important policy has to be to give them jobs. It so 
happens that almost 80 per cent of our unorganised, informal workers, workers who work only 
because they want to avoid starvation, work in conditions of total denigration. There is no job 
security; there is no light or sanitation. These people work in such poor conditions. So, they are 
employed in the sense that when the statistician  

Motion of Thanks  [4 MARCH 2008]  on President's Address   233  
asks them, 'Do you work?', they say, 'yes, we work' . They don't ask them for how much 
money they work, what wages they get, what their working conditions were, and so on. If 
they did, then the entire situation would have been different. So, it is an issue of giving jobs 
to these people.  
Sir, we also find that during this period, particularly during the later part of the period, in 
the organised sector, the factory sector, the growth of employment has practically come to 
zero. Whatever employment has been there in those f actories, in those organized sectors, 
had been of the informal workers, workers who do not have social security, who do not have 
any other protection. They could be called unprotec ted workers. This is the universe, the 
universe which will actually provide livelihood to our poor, to our dalits, to our Muslims, to 
our OBCs. Definitely, I would say, that we must have all those reservation policies, social 
policies. But the first priority should be to give them jobs. How do you do that? I beg to say 
that unfortunately, up till now, in most of our policies, including our planning policies, this 
particular focus is missing. What has happened is t hat if we give particular assistance to 
agriculture, this goes to the larger sops. The poor , small and marginal farms do not get 
credit. Howsoever we may try, howsoever the Reserve Bank of India may dictate banks to 
extend loans, the fact of the matter is, hardly two per cent of the banking credit goes to these 
people. The small and tiny units, which we call sma ll enterprises, contribute about 40 per 
cent of the GDP and they get only less than 4 per c ent of our credit. So, the system has to 
be totally newly worked out with the specific emphasis of programmes for these people. Sir, 
the first important point is that allocation has to  be made and I must congratulate Mr. 
Chidambaram that he has provided allocation. He provided allocation in the last Budget and 
in this Budget he has provided much more than that, and that is the first major condition that 
has been fulfilled. But that is not sufficient. You  have to design programmes in such a 
way that they are actually delivered and the only d esign that will deliver them from the 
examination of the actual statistics is when people involved participate and when there is an 
accountability. Sir, we have seen the Rural Employment Guarantee Scheme. We have seen 
where this scheme has actually worked out. This Sch eme has actually worked out where 
there are proper mechanisms of accountability. In A ndhra Pradesh, they have tried the 
Social Audit System which has been enormously successful and that has to be universalised 
for the country as a whole so that people who are actually getting the benefit or not getting 
the benefit can stand up and say that they must get the benefit. The second most important 
point is that they should be provided as entitlement so that they can claim that, and if they 
do not secure, then there must be something to be done, there must be some compensation 
and somebody should be held responsible. Sir, I am putting it this way because the Rural 
Employment Guarantee Scheme has been talked about and we know what happened and I 
am glad today it has now become accepted. Although initially there were some problems to 
that. But there are certain other schemes.  
The Finance Minister has just left, but if he were here he would have heard me that in his 
Speech he has talked about expanding Health Insurance Scheme. A number of schemes he 
has talked about. Mr. Prasanta Chatterjee talked about the Social Security Bill. The Social 
Security Bill is talking about the national minimum  package of schemes to be given as 
entitlement to workers so that once that is given n obody can withdraw. It is not a scheme 
that the Government in every Budget provides and th en changes. Governments come and 
Governments go, but if it is made into a right or if it is made into an Act, it remains. This is 
what the purpose of this Bill was. In fact, the Sta nding Committee's recommendations are 
built on the scheme that has been announced. If the Government accepts that, there will be

hardly any additional outgo because schemes are alr eady there. But it will give a totally 
different picture. It has mechanism of monitoring; mechanism of evaluation and mechanism 
of dispute settlement. All these things are there in this particular Act.  
Sir, I may mention the other point that has come out which is a very major breakthrough 
for small and marginal farmers and that is debt waiver. I must say that this is not the ideal 
way of dealing with small and marginal farmers. But  this is the first essential step to 
recognise that these small and marginal farmers are  the distressed people and I am very 
happy to say that our Government has announced that  they recognise this. But this is not 
enough. We have to have programmes so that small and marginal farmers can actually get 
benefit. Dr. Swaminathan Report has talked about it; our Report has talked about it. There 
were many such programmes,. During Indira/7's time, we had a Small and Marginal Farmers 
Development Programme. We have to somehow reinvent them and reintroduce them and 
that is the way to go about small and marginal farmers programme.  
Sir, I would like to point out two more things. The  first most important point that we 
learnt from this is that the debts of small and mar ginal farmers are withdrawn. That is not 
sufficient condition that they will get loan again. This is a major point. I want this thing to 
be noted because if you just give up all the debt, you don't get additional money because 
most of the farmers are not paying that. But, they must prepare ground so that they can get 
fresh loans. The banks must get incentives to provi de them loans. Up till now, statistics 
show that the commercial banks do not want to give loans to small and marginal farmers. 
Time and again, when programmes are announced, the small and marginal farmers are 
bypassed. If and when you tell the banks to give th em money without any collateral, the 
farmers do not get loans. And, it is natural. Why should a commercial bank, which is asked 
to make profits, which is asked to minimise its non -performing assets, go and take a risky 
proposition? So, we have to create a particular sys tem by which the banks are actually 
given incentives to provide loans. There is similar ly the question of small units, micro 
units; not the small units having capital of Rs.20 lakh or Rs.25 lakh, but units having capital 
of Rs. 5 lakh or Rs. 10 lakh. Fifty-eight million such units are there in India. They do not get 
any loans. Naturally, a profit-making institution will not be willing to provide them loan. For 
this purpose, in the Common Minimum Programme, we talked about a national fund for the 
unorganised sector. Like NABARD for the agriculture sector, or SIDBI for the small industries, 
the idea was to create a development finance instit ution for the unorganised sector. Sir, in 
this Budget, the Finance Minister has accepted several new development finance agencies. 
But, he has not yet accepted the funding programme for the small and tiny units, that is, the 
national fund for the unorganised sector. I do not know what is the final decision. I would 
expect that the Cabinet should take it into account. For a very simple reason, if you do not 
create an institution, which is solely responsible for this purpose, if you give money to 
SIDBI or NABARD, for example, and tell them that they should also give money to micro 
units, small and large farmers, then, they would no t do that. They would divert all the 
money. You have to create an institution focussed s olely to this particular sector and then 
monitor them as to how they function, provide them money. I am saying this only for the 
simple reason that the time has now come to rethink  our economic strategy. Inclusive 
growth has not been achieved. Economic growth is es sential and I fully agree with Mr. 
Chidambaram when he says that the economic growth gives revenue and you can use that. 
Definitely, that money should be used. But, to use that, we have to have a policy of 
accountability, policy of design, policy of complete change of approach that this is our new 
philosophy of economic development. If we do that, then, definitely, inclusive growth will 
take place in our country.
